catalog_quote: Donohue (n.d.1) presents the Barapasi system of consonantal phonemes, which differs from Bauzi in having /p/ instead of /f/ and adding a glottal stop. The vowel phonemes of Bauzi number six: Table 90: Bauzi vowel phonemes [...] Barapasi lacks the low front vowel, but interestingly is claimed by Donohue (n.d.1) to be tonal, with a minimal tonal contrast of high versus low tone. Bauzi has no gender distinctions for its nouns, unlike the languages further east. Nor are they inflected for number.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere. The only phonological statement on record is that Barapasi is (claimed to be) a tone language with a two-way high vs. low tonal contrast, attributed by Foley to an unpublished Donohue manuscript; nothing is said about stress, its placement, or its relation to tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Foley hedges the tone claim itself ('is claimed by Donohue (n.d.1) to be tonal').
new_statements.domain_note: The sentence was read only as a Google Books search-result snippet of the paywalled chapter (De Gruyter page blocked by a bot check), so surrounding text (e.g. whether tone is lexical or whether any stress remark follows) is unknown. Foley's statement is itself second-hand from Donohue n.d.1; no primary Barapasi phonology has been published. Domain of the tone contrast (word vs. phrase) is not stated in the snippet.
new_statements.identity_note: Wikipedia and Ethnologue spell it Baropasi; Glottolog/Foley use Barapasi; same language bara1375 [brp]. OLAC lists dialect names Marikai and Sipisi (both villages on the Barapasi River); no source specifies which variety Donohue's data represent.
